cards.front: What causes most of Hawaii's weather problems for drivers?
cards.back: Hawaii's weather problems for drivers come mainly from rain, with isolated fog on high-elevation roads and occasional gusty winds, and rain both reduces visibility and changes the road surface.

cards.front: Why are the first few drops of rain dangerous?
cards.back: The first few drops of rain are a danger signal, because the road is most slippery before the oil dropped by passing cars has washed away and oil on water can feel like ice, so slow down, add caution and keep at least double your usual following distance.

cards.front: What is hydroplaning, and how does it start?
cards.back: Prolonged or heavy rain leaves a layer of water on the road, and at speeds up to thirty-five miles per hour tires with good highway tread wipe the surface like a windshield wiper, but at higher speeds the water cannot be cleared and the tires ride up on it like a surfboard, which is called hydroplaning.

cards.front: At what speeds does hydroplaning begin and become complete?
cards.back: Partial hydroplaning may begin at thirty-five miles per hour, it grows with speed and with the amount of water, and at fifty-five miles per hour in heavy rain the tires may lose all contact with the pavement, leaving you unable to brake, accelerate or steer.

cards.front: How can you prevent hydroplaning?
cards.back: To prevent hydroplaning keep good tread depth, because worn or bald tires hydroplane at lower speeds, keep tires at proper pressure, because under-inflated tires hydroplane at lower speeds, and reduce speed, because hydroplaning happens most at higher speeds.

cards.front: How do you dry wet brakes after deep water?
cards.back: After deep water or prolonged heavy rain the brakes may be wet and pull to one side or not hold at all, so reduce speed and apply gentle pedal pressure until they work properly again.

cards.front: How does partial hydroplaning differ from complete loss of contact?
cards.back: Partial hydroplaning can begin at thirty-five miles per hour, while complete loss of tire contact can come at fifty-five miles per hour in heavy rain.

cards.front: How do the first drops of rain differ from prolonged rain?
cards.back: The first drops of rain make the road most slippery because of road oil, while prolonged rain creates the water layer that causes hydroplaning.

cards.front: How does drying wet brakes differ from the flood rule?
cards.back: Wet brakes are dried by gentle pedal pressure at reduced speed, while a flooded road with fast water over one foot deep is never driven through at all.

decks.module: Turn signal rules and the one-hundred-foot law
decks.domain: Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather

cards.front: What does a turn signal give you, and how long must it run?
cards.back: A turn signal shows your intent but gives you no right to make the move, you alone are responsible for making it safely, and traffic regulations require the signal for at least one hundred feet before every turn or lane change and long enough for others to see and understand it.

cards.front: When should you start signaling if you must slow for a turn?
cards.back: If you must slow before a turn or lane change, begin signaling before you slow so other drivers are alerted that you may reduce speed.

cards.front: What are the three rules of turn signals?
cards.back: The three rules of turn signals are to signal every time you intend to turn or change lanes, to begin well in advance so others can see and understand, and to remember that the signal shows intent only and grants no right to move.

cards.front: What are common signaling errors?
cards.back: Common signaling errors are waiting at a red light without signaling the intended turn, signaling too briefly or only after the move has begun, not signaling a right turn, not signaling in a lane that requires a turn, and not signaling because no one seems to be watching.

cards.front: What does failing to signal properly show about a driver?
cards.back: Failing to signal properly is a frequent driver error that shows ignorance, arrogance or uncertainty and a lack of courtesy, and it may mean the driver has no idea what to do next.

cards.front: When must a signal start relative to slowing and distance?
cards.back: Signaling must begin before you slow for a turn, while the signal itself must run for at least one hundred feet before the turn or lane change.

decks.module: Parking on a hill and parking distances
decks.domain: Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather

cards.front: Where should you always park?
cards.back: Always park where the vehicle is clear of traffic and readily visible to approaching drivers, avoiding hidden spots such as just beyond a curve or the crest of a hill.
cards.memory_hook: Clear and visible, not past curves

cards.front: What should you do when parking on a hill?
cards.back: When parking on a hill, always set the hand brake, shift to park if the vehicle has it or otherwise into reverse or low gear, and turn the front wheels toward the curb so that all four wheels would have to climb the curb before the vehicle could roll free.
cards.memory_hook: Brake, park gear, wheels to curb

cards.front: Which way does the manual say to turn the wheels on any hill?
cards.back: Whether you park uphill or downhill, the manual directs you to turn the wheels to the right so that a vehicle that rolls free rolls away from traffic.

cards.front: How close may your bumpers be to other cars when parallel parked?
cards.back: When parallel parked, your front and rear bumpers should be no closer than two feet to the other vehicles unless the street is marked otherwise.

cards.front: Which way must you face, and how close to the curb, when parking?
cards.back: Unless angle parking is clearly designated, you park parallel to the curb facing the direction of traffic, with the curbside wheels no more than twelve inches from the curb or the whole vehicle inside the marked stall.

cards.front: How do the two hill parking wheel directions in the manual differ?
cards.back: On a hill the front wheels go toward the curb so the car cannot roll free, while the manual also directs turning them to the right uphill or downhill so a loose car rolls away from traffic.
cards.memory_hook: Curb stops roll, right avoids traffic

decks.domain: Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather

cards.front: What do four-way hazard flashers mean, and when are they never used?
cards.back: The four-way hazard flashers tell other drivers that your vehicle is stopped in a hazardous spot on the roadway; they must never be used while moving, they show as every turn indicator flashing, and no hand signal exists for them.

cards.front: How do electric stop lamps work?
cards.back: Electric stop lamps operate automatically when the service brake is used, at night their glow should be visible behind the vehicle when you press the pedal, and a hand signal may be used to show braking or slowing.

cards.front: Why must you know hand signals?
cards.back: Hand signals remain an accepted way to show intentions and knowing them is required in case the electric signals fail, their only advantage being that they are seldom subject to failure.

cards.front: What are the drawbacks of hand signals?
cards.back: Hand signals are hard to tell from other arm motions, hard to see in darkness and bad weather, not readily visible to drivers on the right, require an open window, and leave only one hand on the wheel.

cards.front: How long have vehicles had electric signals?
cards.back: Electric stop signals have been standard for more than fifty years, most vehicles built since the early nineteen fifties have electric turn signals, and since nineteen sixty-eight every vehicle has had electric turn, stop and four-way hazard signals.

cards.front: What are the advantages of electric signals?
cards.back: Electric signals can be operated instantly from a closed vehicle, are visible in darkness and bad weather and from all angles except the immediate sides, are seldom misinterpreted, and leave both hands free for control.

cards.front: What are the disadvantages of electric signals?
cards.back: The disadvantages of electric signals are failure to cancel and failure to function, and a failure to cancel usually comes from a turn or lane change too small to trip the self-cancelling mechanism combined with the driver not watching the panel indicator, whose abnormal behavior is the clue to a signal problem.
cards.memory_hook: Fail to cancel, fail to work

cards.front: How do hazard flashers differ from turn signals in use?
cards.back: Hazard flashers warn of a vehicle stopped in a hazardous position and are never used while moving, while turn signals are used for every turn and lane change while moving.

cards.front: How do electric signals compare with hand signals?
cards.back: Electric signals can fail to cancel or fail to work, while hand signals rarely fail but are hard to see at night, from the right side and through a closed window.

cards.front: What should you do when heavy rain cuts visibility?
cards.back: When heavy rain cuts visibility even with the wipers running, reduce speed and turn on the low-beam head lamps so others can see you, and if you still cannot see clearly, pull onto the shoulder or another clear area and stop until the rain lets up.

cards.front: What are the rules about flooded roads and moving water?
cards.back: Avoid driving through flooded areas because you may be stranded, and never drive through swiftly moving water more than one foot deep, which will sweep the vehicle off the road.

cards.front: Where does fog occur in Hawaii, and why are patches hazardous?
cards.back: Fog in Hawaii almost never occurs at low elevations but can meet the road at higher elevations where low clouds touch the ground, and patches of fog are especially hazardous because they appear suddenly.

cards.front: How should you drive in fog, and when must you stop?
cards.back: In fog, sharply reduce speed and use low beams, never high beams, whose reflection reduces your own vision and the approaching driver's, be ready for an emergency stop, and if you cannot see at least two car lengths, about forty feet, pull completely off the pavement, stop and turn on the hazard signals.
cards.memory_hook: Low beams, forty feet, pull off

cards.front: What does the manual advise about winter driving elsewhere?
cards.back: Winter driving elsewhere brings hazards unknown in Hawaii, and unless experienced you should avoid it, otherwise fit snow tread tires, start slowly and test the brakes gently once moving, keep the windows clear of snow, ice and frost, keep a safe distance and watch for vehicles in trouble, drive slower and stay on the clear dry parts of the road.

cards.front: Why use low beams rather than high beams in fog?
cards.back: Low beams are the rule in both fog and heavy rain, while high beams in fog reflect back and blind both you and the oncoming driver.

cards.front: When must you stop in fog versus in heavy rain?
cards.back: In fog you stop when you cannot see two car lengths, about forty feet, while in heavy rain you stop whenever you cannot see clearly even with the wipers on.

decks.domain: Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather

cards.front: How do you angle park?
cards.back: For angle parking, keep safe clearance and drive forward into the space with equal room on each side between the lines.

cards.front: How do you begin parallel parking?
cards.back: Parallel parking begins by signaling and stopping even with the front car about eighteen inches from it with the rear bumpers even, then backing slowly with the wheel turned sharply right until the car is at about a forty-five degree angle to the street, then quickly straightening the front wheels and backing slowly.

cards.front: How do you finish parallel parking?
cards.back: When your front bumper is even with the other car's rear bumper, turn the wheel sharply and rapidly all the way left and back slowly toward the car behind without touching it, then turn sharply right, pull forward slowly and center the car in the space.

cards.front: What distances apply when parallel parking?
cards.back: Parallel parking starts eighteen inches from the front car and ends with bumpers at least two feet from the neighbors, while the curbside wheels must finish within twelve inches of the curb.

decks.module: Sharing the road and motorcycle lane rights
decks.domain: Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather

cards.front: How do large vehicles compare with small vehicles on the road?
cards.back: You share the road with trucks, buses, cars, motorcycles, bicycles and pedestrians, and larger vehicles protect their occupants more and are easier to see but harder to operate, while small vehicles protect less and are less visible but more agile.

cards.front: What should you watch for regarding other vehicles' limits?
cards.back: Recognize the capabilities and limits of other vehicles and your own, look carefully for smaller vehicles such as motorcycles and bicycles, and make sure the drivers of trucks and buses can see you.
cards.memory_hook: Spot small, be seen by big

cards.front: How should you treat motorcyclists, bicyclists and pedestrians?
cards.back: Give motorcyclists, bicyclists and pedestrians plenty of room and look for them with extra care when turning or changing lanes, and a motorcyclist is entitled to the entire width of the traffic lane.
cards.memory_hook: Give room, full lane for motorcycles

cards.front: What are the trade-offs between large and small vehicles?
cards.back: Larger vehicles are easier to see but harder to operate, while smaller vehicles are more agile but less visible and less protective.

decks.domain: Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather

cards.front: Above what speed will most automatic transmissions refuse to downshift?
cards.back: Most automatic transmissions downshift when the selector is moved to the next lower position, but above about sixty miles per hour they will not, so the vehicle must first slow before an automatic transmission can downshift.

cards.front: Why is routine downshifting to slow down not recommended?
cards.back: Routine downshifting to slow down is not recommended because it decelerates the vehicle sharply without lighting the stop lamps to warn following drivers, so downshifting to reduce speed should only supplement the brakes.

cards.front: What happens when you floor the accelerator at highway speed, and what does abuse cost?
cards.back: At normal highway speeds every passenger car automatic transmission downshifts by itself when the accelerator is fully depressed, downshifting at higher speeds may actually reduce the vehicle's ability to accelerate, and abusing the technique stresses the engine and transmission and can lead to costly repairs.

cards.front: When is downshifting a proper emergency procedure, and what needs care?
cards.back: Downshifting is a proper emergency procedure for slowing a vehicle after partial or complete brake failure, but it needs extra care on a slippery surface because the unequal forces it creates can cause control problems.

cards.front: When is downshifting proper, and when is it discouraged?
cards.back: Downshifting is proper as an emergency measure after brake failure and before a steep downgrade, while downshifting as a routine way to slow is discouraged because following drivers get no stop-lamp warning.
